headline: A CMP client can accept a key pair the CA generated for it, and refuses one from an authority that never claimed to be one.
summary:
An end entity that cannot generate its own key pair asks the CA to generate it centrally, and the CA delivers it in the enrollment response: an RFC 5958 key package, signed by a Key Generation Authority, sealed to the entity that asked. pki.cmp.openKeyPackage opens that container and hands back the private key, and pki.cmp.session accepts one when the caller says it wants one.

RFC 9483 requires the authority to hold a certificate asserting id-kp-cmKGA in order to be accepted as one. That is an assertion the certificate has to make, not a constraint it merely has to satisfy: under RFC 5280 a certificate with no extendedKeyUsage extension permits every purpose, so treating the purpose as a path-validation constraint would let a certificate that says nothing about key generation deliver a private key. Both halves are checked, and no key material is returned until they pass.

Added: pki.cmp.openKeyPackage(container, opts) opens a centrally generated private key delivered in a CMP response (RFC 9483 section 4.1.6). The container is the CMS EnvelopedData a CA puts in the privateKey field of a granted CertifiedKeyPair, holding a CMS SignedData over an RFC 5958 AsymmetricKeyPackage. Both layers are undone in order and the authority is authorized before any key material is returned. The result is { keys, kga, trusted }: keys is every OneAsymmetricKey in the package, in order, each its own DER Buffer that is a PKCS#8 PrivateKeyInfo ready for pki.key.import; kga is the signer certificate whose signature was checked; trusted says whether that certificate chained. Each element is parsed as a OneAsymmetricKey before it is surfaced, so a SEQUENCE carrying neither an algorithm nor key octets is refused rather than handed back as a key.

Both CMS layers are accepted in either form they are seen in. A ContentInfo opens with the OBJECT IDENTIFIER naming its content type; the bare structure opens with its own CMSVersion INTEGER. A CMP EncryptedKey carries the EnvelopedData itself (RFC 9810 section 5.2.2), and RFC 5652 section 6.1 encrypts the content rather than a ContentInfo around it, so the plaintext under an id-signedData encryptedContentInfo is a SignedData. The two forms are structurally exclusive, so neither is guessed at.

Which key management technique opens the container follows the protection of the request that asked for the key. opts.key, with an optional opts.cert, opens the key transport and key agreement containers a signature-protected request selects (sections 4.1.6.1 and 4.1.6.2); opts.password opens the password container a MAC-protected request selects (section 4.1.6.3). The shared secret is copied at the door and wiped when the call returns, whether the container opened or not.

The key generation authority is authorized on both of the section's terms. Its certificate must chain to an anchor in opts.trustAnchors, and it must assert the id-kp-cmKGA extended key usage (RFC 9480 section 2.2). A certificate carrying no extendedKeyUsage extension satisfies a requiredEku path constraint, since RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.12 constrains a certificate only when the extension is present, so the assertion is checked separately: an absent, empty, or differently-purposed extension does not authorize. The chain is still held to requiredEku as well, which reaches the intermediates an issuer's own extended key usage constrains.

opts.trustAnchors and opts.intermediates each take one certificate or a list of them, as DER or PEM, the way pki.cmp.verify takes them. A pki.cmp.session forwards both of its own pools the same way, including an already-parsed certificate, which it hands on as the bytes it was parsed from, and the { name, publicKey, algorithm } anchor tuple, which it passes through; a certificate that went missing on the way would make the authority's chain unbuildable and read as an unauthorized authority.

opts.authorizedBySharedSecret states the exemption section 4.1.6 gives an entity that protected its request with a shared secret, which MAY authorize the authority by that secret instead of validating its certificate. It applies only to a container opened with opts.password, it refuses opts.trustAnchors so that one call names one authorization rule, and the result reports trusted: false.

pki.cmp.session takes opts.acceptCentralKeyGeneration, which drives the whole exchange rather than only the response. The request goes out in the shape section 4.1.6 defines: a certTemplate with no publicKey, or one whose subjectPublicKey is a zero-length BIT STRING stating an algorithm preference, and no proof of possession, since this entity holds no key to prove possession of. It carries cmp2021 in its header, because the response will carry an EnvelopedData (RFC 9480 section 2.20), and so does every later leg of that transaction: a poll asking for the grant expects the EnvelopedData just as the request did, and a resumed poll in a later process is the same transaction. The session then opens the delivered container with the credential it enrolled under, authorizes the authority against the anchors it already holds at the instant opts.time names, and surfaces the result on the enrollment verdict as deliveredKey. A shared-secret session with no anchors authorizes by its secret. An enrollment that delivered no key reports deliveredKey: null. Without the option, such a request is refused before it is sent and such a grant is refused with cmp/unexpected-arm.

The issued certificate must certify the delivered private key, checked before the certConf that would accept the grant. The authority's signature says the key package is authentic and says nothing about which certificate the key belongs with, so a mismatched pair is cmp/bad-key-package: the certificate would be unusable with the key the enrollment received. A central key generation transaction submits no public key of its own, so the delivered key is the only thing its grant is bound to, and a granted CertResponse that carries no privateKey is cmp/bad-cert-response rather than a confirmed issuance.

The pair is proven by USING it, not by deriving the public half and comparing. A key structure states its own public half and the key engine reads what it is told: RFC 5958 section 2 gives a OneAsymmetricKey an optional publicKey, an EC key's RFC 5915 ECPrivateKey carries its own public point, and an RSA private key carries the modulus and public exponent outright, so a structure whose private components were replaced while its stored public ones were left alone derives to exactly the public key planted in it. Instead the two halves perform whichever operation the key type can: a signature the public half verifies (RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA), a Diffie-Hellman agreement reached from both sides (X25519, X448), or a key encapsulation the private half decapsulates (ML-KEM). What that establishes is that the delivered key works with the issued certificate; it is not a statement that every field of the private structure is internally consistent, which no operation reveals.

One RSA key pair may be identified either by rsaEncryption or by id-RSASSA-PSS (RFC 4055 section 1.2), and the authority that encodes a delivered key need not have chosen what the CA put in the certificate. The key engine reports those two encodings as different key types, so the pair is recognized as one algorithm and exercised under PSS, the padding the restricted encoding permits, honoring any hash and salt length that encoding pins. A different modulus under the same cross-encoding is still refused.

A central key generation transaction that outlives its process resumes like any other. Its resumeToken records that the grant is bound to the delivered key rather than to a requested one, and carries no requestedSpki, since there is no requested key. A session resuming it must set opts.acceptCentralKeyGeneration too, and a token naming both bindings, or neither, is refused.

pki.schema.cmp.parse surfaces the encoded EnvelopedData of a CertifiedKeyPair privateKey as certifiedKeyPair.privateKey.bytes, alongside the walked structure, so the container can be opened from the bytes the response carried rather than from a re-serialization.
The RFC 5958 asymmetric key package content type is registered in the OID registry as aKeyPackage (2.16.840.1.101.2.1.2.78.5).
Fixed: pki.cmp.build sets cmp2021 on an ir / cr / kur that asks for central key generation. RFC 9480 section 2.20 needs the version when a message exchange uses EnvelopedData, "for the request being sent or for the expected response", and RFC 9483 section 4.1.6 requires it in the header "already for the initial request message". A request carrying a real public key, with or without a proof of possession, still goes out as cmp2000.

pki.cmp.session claims its one transaction slot before it reads the caller's request object. Reading such an object runs whatever accessors it carries, and an accessor can call back into the same session; a slot claimed only after validation let that re-entrant call open a transaction the outer call then wrote its own state over. The re-entrant call is now refused with cmp/bad-input, on enroll, revoke, info and resumePoll alike. A request refused during validation still leaves the session retryable, as before.

pki.cmp.session.enroll sends the arm it checked. The request arm and its certTemplate are copied out of the caller's object once, so a field that answers differently on a second read cannot turn a validated client-generated enrollment into a central key generation request the session never admitted. enroll also names an unrecognized request field itself, with cmp/bad-input, rather than leaving it to be dropped.
Changed: The container is held to RFC 9483 section 4.1.6 wherever its shape decides who can read the key or what the signature covers: it must be an EnvelopedData, it must name exactly one RecipientInfo, its encrypted content type must be id-signedData, and the signed content type must be id-ct-KP-aKeyPackage. A second recipient is a second party able to open a key generated for this entity, and the count is read past the RecipientInfo: one KeyAgreeRecipientInfo wraps the content-encryption key once per entry in its recipientEncryptedKeys, each for a different recipient (RFC 5652 section 6.2.2), so a container naming one of those with two entries is refused too. The signed content type is what binds the signature to a key package rather than to whatever else the authority has signed. The section's CMS version literals are not enforced, because RFC 5652 section 5.1 and section 6.1 derive those from the signer and recipient forms in use and a conforming sender reaches different values; nor are its choice-of-form rules (the signer identifier form, certificate ordering), which are surfaced for a caller with a stricter profile to judge. The number of keys in the package is held where it decides something: section 4.1.6 gives the eContent a sequence of one, and a pki.cmp.session enrollment requires that, since one grant certifies one key and every further key is one the issued certificate says nothing about. pki.cmp.openKeyPackage on its own surfaces a whole RFC 5958 AsymmetricKeyPackage, which is SIZE (1..MAX), and leaves the binding to its caller.
